title: Nucleophilic substitution
goal: How a nucleophile replaces a leaving group at a saturated carbon: SN2, SN1, and making leaving groups.

problemSets.title: SN2: one concerted step
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group leaves, in one step.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In **SN2** the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon from the side **opposite** the leaving group, and the C–X bond breaks **at the same time**: two arrows, one step.

- Rate = k[nucleophile][substrate]: both take part in the slow step.
- Best on **methyl and primary** carbons, and fast on benzylic ones; a tertiary carbon is too crowded.
- A stereocentre is **inverted**.
- Good nucleophiles: I⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, amines. Polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMSO, DMF) speed it up.

setItems.whyThisOne: The pattern: two arrows, one step.
A carbon nucleophile makes a C–C bond.
Halide exchange, driven by a precipitate.
A neutral nucleophile: SN2, then a proton transfer.

problemSets.title: SN1: the carbocation first
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The leaving group goes first; a nucleophile then captures a flat carbocation.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In **SN1** the C–X bond breaks **on its own** (the slow step), giving a **carbocation**, which a nucleophile then captures.

- Rate = k[substrate]: the nucleophile is not in the slow step.
- Needs a **stable cation**: tertiary, benzylic or allylic. Typical nucleophiles are weak ones such as water or an alcohol, often the solvent.
- The cation is flat, so a stereocentre is **racemised**.
- An **allylic** cation can be attacked at either end, and a cation can **rearrange** (a 1,2-hydride shift) to a more stable one first.
- After water or an alcohol adds, a **proton transfer** gives the neutral product.

setItems.whyThisOne: The three steps of SN1 at a tertiary carbon.
Two rings stabilise a secondary cation.
One cation, two ends: two products.
The cation rearranges before bromide arrives.

problemSets.title: Making leaving groups
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: OH is a poor leaving group: protonate it, or turn it into OTs or O–P⁺.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Hydroxide is a strong base, so **OH never leaves on its own**. Turn it into something that leaves as a weak base:

- **Protonate** it with HBr: water leaves.
- Make a **tosylate** with TsCl and pyridine. The C–O bond is not touched, so the configuration is kept; TsO⁻ then leaves about as well as a halide.
- Bond it to **phosphorus** (the Appel reaction: PPh₃, CBr₄). Ph₃P=O leaves, driven by the strong P=O bond.

The last step is then an ordinary SN2, or SN1 on a tertiary carbon.

setItems.whyThisOne: Acid makes the leaving group; SN2 on a primary carbon.
Substitution at sulfur: the carbon keeps its configuration.
Four steps, driven by the P=O bond.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: SN2 or SN1? Decide from the carbon, the nucleophile and the leaving group.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: SN1 at a stabilised secondary carbon.
